name: Canthopexy

lead: Canthopexy anchors the lateral canthal tendon to lift and support the lower eyelid without cutting the lid margin. Surgeons use it with lower blepharoplasty to limit lid malposition.
Looksmaxxers discuss it for canthal tilt and almond eye shape, usually as an alternative to canthoplasty.

paras: A suture secures the lateral canthal tendon to the orbital rim, giving the lower lid support and a slight lateral lift. Canthoplasty differs by cutting the canthus.

Surgical papers connect lower lid surgery with lid malposition and use canthal support to reduce that risk; ectropion prevention is itself a studied use. Forum members disagree about how long results last.

lead: Canthopexy is a surgical procedure that tightens or repositions the lower eyelid by anchoring the lateral canthal tendon, without cutting the eyelid margin at the outer corner. Surgical papers present it as a routine companion to lower blepharoplasty that restores lid tone and contour and reduces the chance of lower lid malposition [1][2].

A 1993 paper argued canthopexy should be a routine part of or alternative to lower lid blepharoplasty [1], and a 10-year review of lower blepharoplasty with routine lateral canthal support reported on outcomes with that approach [3]. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to improve canthal tilt and eye shape, and is often compared with canthoplasty [4][5].
infobox: Support during lower blepharoplasty; ectropion prevention
Better canthal tilt, almond or fox eye shape

paras: Wikipedia defines canthoplasty as plastic surgery of the medial and/or lateral canthus and says it is used in cosmetic procedures and in procedures addressing eyelid function or malposition; it does not mention canthopexy by name [6]. Surgical authors distinguish canthopexy, a suture-based support, from canthoplasty, which involves cutting the canthus [7]. An algorithm for choosing between them was published in 1999, including a simplified suture canthopexy called the lateral retinacular suspension [7].
Anatomical work describes the ligamentous attachments of the lower lid and lateral canthus, which form the basis for these procedures [8].

Published studies are mainly surgical case series and anatomical work. They include a 10-year review of lower blepharoplasty with routine lateral canthal support [3], a paper on the lateral transorbital canthopexy for correction and prevention of ectropion with a grading system and outcome study [9], and a paper on lateral canthal anchoring [10]. A registered trial (NCT07775417) compares two ectropion-prevention measures in orbital fracture surgery and has not yet started recruiting [11]. No study found tests canthopexy for improving canthal tilt in people seeking appearance change.

On looksmax.org, threads ask whether to choose canthopexy or canthoplasty for canthal tilt, noting conflicting online advice that canthoplasty is for people over 30 [4]. One member argues canthopexy is preferable, particularly under 40, because it does not cut the lower eyelid, while another says it may relax after a year or two [5]. Others ask whether pulling the lateral corner adds millimeters of positive fixed lid length [12].

lore.intro: Canthopexy is discussed on looksmax.org as a milder alternative to canthoplasty for eye shape and canthal tilt [4][5].

claims.claim: Canthopexy gives a better almond or fox eye than canthoplasty.
Canthopexy results relax back within a year or two.

timeline.event: A paper argues canthopexy should be a routine part of or alternative to lower lid blepharoplasty [1].
An algorithm for canthoplasty and the lateral retinacular suspension, a simplified suture canthopexy, is published [7].
A 10-year review reports on lower blepharoplasty with routine lateral canthal support [3].
